explanations.explanation: That's him, baker. The passage says Pharaoh Neco's army was defeated at Carchemish on the Euphrates River by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 46:2). It also says this happened in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, Judah's king. Neco showed up with an army and left with a very long story to avoid telling.

Sennacherib was a king of Assyria, and he's a real name from Bible history, so I see why it pulled you. But the verse names someone else. Jeremiah 46:2 says Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated Neco's army at Carchemish. Right place, wrong king, and that happens to the best of us.

Cyrus was king of Persia, and he shows up later in the Bible's story. He isn't the one here, friend. Jeremiah 46:2 says Neco's army was defeated at Carchemish by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. Cyrus wasn't even in this fight.

Yes, baker. The LORD asks, "Why am I seeing this?" and then says, "They are terrified, they are retreating; their warriors are defeated…" (Jeremiah 46:5). After all those shiny orders, this is the scene He describes. Big plans, then a big U-turn.

That's what the orders sound like they're heading toward, I'll give you that. But the LORD describes the opposite. "They are terrified, they are retreating; their warriors are defeated…" (Jeremiah 46:5). No victory march anywhere in this verse.

Waiting around would be a calmer scene, friend. The verse is not calm at all. It says "They are terrified, they are retreating…" and "terror is on every side!" (Jeremiah 46:5). Nobody is standing at ease.

Not quite, baker. You'd think the fast ones would at least make it out, but the text says the opposite: "The swift cannot flee, and the warrior cannot escape!" (Jeremiah 46:6). It adds that they stumble and fall by the River Euphrates in the north. Being the fastest didn't save anybody here.

Right, baker. Jeremiah 46:6 says, "The swift cannot flee, and the warrior cannot escape!" They stumble and fall in the north by the River Euphrates. I'd have trained for this day my whole life and still not made it out.

That's right. "Egypt rises like the Nile, and its waters churn like rivers…" (Jeremiah 46:8). The question in verse 7 gets answered right there. It's a picture of a river swelling up, and that's how Egypt carries itself.

Babylon is the one who won at Carchemish, so I see why you went there. But the river-rising picture isn't about Babylon. Jeremiah 46:8 says, "Egypt rises like the Nile…" The rising belongs to Egypt, and the passage shows where that rising ends up.

Assyria doesn't show up anywhere in these verses, friend. The one rising is named outright: "Egypt rises like the Nile, and its waters churn like rivers…" (Jeremiah 46:8). And a Nile comparison fits Egypt, since the Nile is Egypt's river.

explanations.answer: Cover the earth and destroy cities
explanations.explanation: Yep. Egypt boasts, "I will rise and cover the earth; I will destroy the cities and their people." (Jeremiah 46:8). That is a LOT of talk from a river. Big words, and the passage tells us where they go.

explanations.answer: Build a wall around its borders
explanations.explanation: A wall would be a quiet, keep-to-yourself kind of plan. This boast is the opposite of quiet. Egypt says, "I will rise and cover the earth; I will destroy the cities and their people." (Jeremiah 46:8). That's walls coming down, not going up.

I wish it were that friendly, baker, but no. The boast in Jeremiah 46:8 is, "I will rise and cover the earth; I will destroy the cities and their people." Nothing about peace. That boast comes with a big flood and zero handshakes.
That's the list. "Cush and Put carrying their shields, men of Lydia drawing the bow." (Jeremiah 46:9). Shields from two places and archers from the third. That's a whole crowd answering the call.

Those three are neighbors of Israel, so they're easy to grab for. But they aren't in this verse. Jeremiah 46:9 names "Cush and Put carrying their shields, men of Lydia drawing the bow." Different map, friend.

Those are names from the east, and they sound very warrior-ish, I know. But the verse lists other places. Jeremiah 46:9 says, "Cush and Put carrying their shields, men of Lydia drawing the bow." Shields from Cush and Put, bows from Lydia.

Right. "For that day belongs to the Lord GOD of Hosts, a day of vengeance against His foes." (Jeremiah 46:10). It's His day, not Egypt's. This one is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly and let it stand.

Celebration is a happy word, and this verse isn't happy. The text says it is "a day of vengeance against His foes." (Jeremiah 46:10). Nobody is passing out cookies on this day, and I'd know, because I'd be the one stamping them.

Rest sounds peaceful, baker, but the verse goes another way. It calls that day "a day of vengeance against His foes." (Jeremiah 46:10). It also says the sword will devour, so nobody is putting their feet up.

Yes. "For the Lord GOD of Hosts will hold a sacrifice in the land of the north by the River Euphrates." (Jeremiah 46:10). That's the word the text uses. It's a heavy picture, so I'll just say it's the LORD speaking and leave it there.

A trial would at least have a judge's bench and a lot of paperwork. But the verse uses a different word. It says the Lord GOD of Hosts "will hold a sacrifice in the land of the north by the River Euphrates." (Jeremiah 46:10).

A census is just counting heads, friend, and this verse is not counting anybody. It says, "For the Lord GOD of Hosts will hold a sacrifice in the land of the north by the River Euphrates." (Jeremiah 46:10). Different kind of event entirely.

That's it. "In vain you try many remedies, but for you there is no healing." (Jeremiah 46:11). Egypt is told to try Gilead's balm and the verse says it won't work. I think that's a hard line to hear, so I'll just say it plain.

Shelter fits a battle scene, I get it. But the word in the verse is about a wound. "In vain you try many remedies, but for you there is no healing." (Jeremiah 46:11). Balm is for hurts, not for roofs.

Pardon is a word for forgiveness, and that isn't the one here. The verse talks about balm and remedies, so the word is about a wound. It says, "In vain you try many remedies, but for you there is no healing." (Jeremiah 46:11).

Yes, baker. "The nations have heard of your shame, and your outcry fills the earth…" (Jeremiah 46:12). Word gets around. It's the kind of news that travels faster than a batch of fresh cookies hits the cooling rack.
Not this time, friend. The text says, "The nations have heard of your shame, and your outcry fills the earth…" (Jeremiah 46:12). So the nations do hear about it. Nobody keeps this one quiet.

explanations.answer: Her warriors stumble over each other and fall
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. The outcry fills the earth "because warrior stumbles over warrior and both of them have fallen together." (Jeremiah 46:12). It's a pile-up, friend. I'd have paid good money to not be standing there.

explanations.answer: Her cities are flooded by the Nile
explanations.explanation: The Nile does show up in this passage, but only as a picture of Egypt rising. The reason for the outcry is different. It's "because warrior stumbles over warrior and both of them have fallen together." (Jeremiah 46:12).

explanations.answer: Her king is carried off as a captive
explanations.explanation: That would be a big event, and I can see why you'd pick it. But this passage doesn't say it. The outcry comes "because warrior stumbles over warrior and both of them have fallen together." (Jeremiah 46:12). Only the warriors are named as the reason.
